heading: Things I'm building
intro: Beeline controls my Mac from typed or spoken requests. Observatory shows where my AI limits and spend went, and when the limits run out. Career Bridge surveys workers on how they use AI, and cube·type turns a Rubik’s cube into a typing game.

projects.name: Beeline
projects.tagline: A Mac assistant that acts on typed or spoken requests, and a small bee shows each action first.
projects.summary: I open it with ⌘Space, then type, or hold the keys and talk. It opens things, changes settings, presses buttons and runs short plans.

film.label: Beeline on a Mac: a request is typed into the Beeline bar, then a bee flies to a TextEdit toolbar button and presses it

sections.title: What it does
body: Beeline opens apps, files, tabs and System Settings pages from everyday words like “night shift”. It also runs menu commands, presses buttons in the app in front, tiles windows, converts units and currencies, and handles file chores like compressing or moving what’s selected in Finder.

Holding ⌘Space turns the search field into a microphone. My words fill the bar as I speak, and Return runs the top result. For bigger requests it asks Claude for a short plan, shows every step, and runs nothing until I approve it.

sections.title: The bee
body: Before Beeline presses something, a small drawn bee flies from the bar to the button, menu or window, a ring settles on the target, and a label says what is about to happen. My real pointer never moves.

Escape stops a run from any app, and clicking or typing myself takes over. Anything that can’t be undone, like emptying the Trash, pressing Send or a dialog’s OK, needs Return twice, and the card says what it will touch.

sections.title: Where it came from
body: Voice control started as a separate prototype. I merged it into Beeline so one bar handles typing and talking, and kept two of its ideas: the on-screen cursor and a safe way to stop a run.

highlights: Uses Apple’s on-device model for loose requests, and learns what I pick
Stops a run on Escape and still passes the key to the app in front
Follow-ups like “undo that” and “the other window” work typed or spoken
Runs on the Mac and goes online only for currency rates and requests I send to Claude

connects.text: Plans come from Claude, and Observatory shows how much of that usage is left.

projects.name: Observatory
projects.kind: Menu bar app and dashboard · Mac, Windows and Linux
projects.tagline: A menu bar app and dashboard that shows which sessions used my Claude Code and Codex limits, what each one shipped, and when each limit runs out.
projects.summary: Each limit says when it runs out at my current pace, or that it has room. Seven dashboard views show sessions, limits, tokens and screen time over a day up to all time. It runs on my own computer and doesn't change any of the tools it reads.

film.label: Observatory's limit history with fictional data, switching between 7-day and 30-day charts for Claude Code and Codex 5-hour and weekly limits.

sections.title: Run out, or room
body: Each limit window is forecast once per reading, and the dashboard, menu bar and tray all show that same sentence, like “Claude runs out Wed 3–7 PM at this pace” or “has room”. The pace ignores readings from before a reset, and once a few days of readings are stored it gives a range taken from how far its own earlier forecasts missed. A window that has only just reset says it is too early to forecast.

The menu bar and tray icon is a ring that fills as the weekly limit is used. A dot in the center means it lasts until the reset, and a bar means it runs out first. An engine that is signed out, on a free plan, or has had no reading for a day reads Off, not an old number.

sections.title: Seven views
body: Overview, Sessions, Limits, Tokens, Screen time, Drift and Settings share one scope bar. It picks the computers and sources, and a period from a day to all time. Overview shows spend, branches merged and commits on main for the week, each against the previous period, and every number opens into its parts.
Sessions reads as “[Builder] Lantern”: a role and what it worked on, with its computer, models, spend and commits on main. Repeated runs fold into one row.

sections.title: Ask a question
body: An Ask field and pinned questions such as “Where did today's spend go?” rearrange the same blocks on the screen. Nothing in the dashboard calls a model. An optional MCP server lets my own Claude client compose a view and save it. It can't read my usage, and a saved view holds queries, never numbers or session titles.

sections.title: History
body: History goes back to the first day each source has data, and a day stays counted after Claude Code deletes its old transcripts. Dollar figures are estimates at public API prices, not a bill.

sections.title: Monitor only
body: It doesn't start, stop or answer an agent, and it doesn't change the tools it reads. It sends nothing to any server and has no telemetry. Saved data holds no prompts, responses or window titles.
It shows missing data as Unknown, not zero.

sections.title: Status for agents
body: One command prints the same limits as JSON for scripts and agents: percent left, reset time, burn rate and pace for each window, and which engine to send a task to. It can also wait for an engine that ran out to reach its reset time. It reads saved data on this computer, makes no network calls and writes nothing.

sections.title: Several computers
body: Setup is one command. It builds the dashboard and a small menu bar app on my own computer and starts them at login, with no account and no installer. A Mac, a Windows PC and a Linux computer can share one view over SSH, and the dashboard labels combined sums as not deduplicated.

highlights: Claude Code and Codex limits sit side by side, and Grok is optional
Screen time from ActivityWatch, grouped by app and category
Tests plant fake prompts and keys in session logs and check none come out in Observatory’s data
Tests run on macOS, Windows and Linux
MIT licensed, with a demo that uses fictional data

connects.text: Tracks the Claude limits that Beeline’s plans use.

projects.name: Career Bridge
projects.tagline: A survey of how Massachusetts workers use AI at work, built with a team at a datathon.
projects.summary: It won 3rd place at the Human Edge Studio datathon by SG+I. Job ads show what employers ask for, not what people in the job do with AI, so Career Bridge asks them and publishes only totals.

sections.title: The gap
body: About 526,000 Massachusetts workers are in jobs where AI overlaps with much of the work, yet under 1% of job ads for those jobs mention AI skills. These figures come from the Lightcast AI Exposure Index, 2025 job ads and BLS worker counts.
Ads can’t tell the difference between a job that doesn’t need AI and one where people already use it and nobody is asking. Asking people can.

sections.title: The survey
body: Workers take five minutes to mark which work activities they do in a typical week and whether AI helps with each. Employers take three to say what the role needs and what is becoming more important.

The activities come from O*NET, so answers line up with federal data, plus three AI activities O*NET doesn’t track yet. It starts with three jobs: administrative assistants, customer service representatives and retail salespeople.

sections.title: Results and job pages
body: Results show only totals by job and region, and hide any group with fewer than 10 responses. The page points out where workers and employers differ, which shows who could use AI training.
Career counselors can look up any job for pay, growth, training, how much AI is already used on the work, and nearby jobs with similar skills. Every number names its source.

sections.title: Status
body: Career Bridge is a working prototype, and all survey results in the demo are sample data. It’s an independent student project, not affiliated with MassHire, Lightcast or the Commonwealth of Massachusetts.

projects.name: cube·type
projects.tagline: A typing game where every word turns a Rubik’s cube.
projects.summary: Every turn of the cube has a word: type rush and the right face turns, type recoil and it turns back. It plays in the browser and keeps stats like a typing test.

film.label: cube·type close-up: typing roam and unfurl with Enter turns the right and top faces of a Rubik's cube twice each, repeating until the cube is back where it started.

sections.title: How it plays
body: The first letter of a word is its face, words about going forward turn clockwise, and words about going back turn counter-clockwise. Enter repeats the last turn, so a word then Enter is a double. Swiping or the arrow keys rotate the whole cube.
The bar at the top tracks each stage of a CFOP solve. Once the first two layers are done, the last-layer algorithm shows up as a line of words to type, like a Monkeytype test.

sections.title: Three modes
body: Drill shows one move at a time and asks for its word. Sprint is one timed solve with splits. Zen is untimed, and new cubes keep coming.
Typing is never corrected. Wrong letters stay in red until I delete them, and a turn happens only when the word is exact.

sections.title: Choosing the words
body: Each move has a pool of words, and a picker chooses which one shows. Like Monkeytype it is mostly random, but it leans toward short words that switch hands and avoid using the same finger twice in a row.
It also counts finesse, borrowed from Tetris: turns that cancel out, like R then R prime, are wasted, and the game flags them.

highlights: Stats for best time, average of 5 and 12, splits and finesse, saved in the browser
Eight camera views, and words move to sit beside their faces
Four themes, including the classic Monkeytype look
